items.prompt: What is the term for arranging elements so the viewer knows what to read or notice first, second and third?

options.label: Print bleed margin
Letter-pair kerning
Visual hierarchy
Color gamut range

rubric: Visual hierarchy is the ordering of elements by importance.
Kerning is letter-pair spacing, bleed is a print margin and gamut is a color range.

items.prompt: In typography, what does kerning refer to?

options.label: The space between lines of text
The width of a column of text
The thickness of a letter's strokes
The space between two letters

rubric: Kerning adjusts the space between individual letter pairs.
Line spacing is leading, which is the usual confusion.

items.prompt: Which set lists the primary colors of the RGB model used on screens?

options.label: Cyan, magenta, yellow
Red, yellow, blue
Orange, green, purple
Red, green, blue

rubric: RGB uses red, green and blue light.
Red, yellow, blue is traditional paint and cyan, magenta, yellow is the print model.

items.prompt: Which of these typefaces is a serif typeface?

options.label: Times New Roman
Helvetica
Arial
Futura

rubric: Times New Roman has small strokes at letter ends, which makes it serif.
The others are sans-serif.

items.prompt: What is white space (negative space) in a design?

options.label: The blank margin that gets added at print time
Any part of the layout that is filled with white
The empty area around and between elements
The area set aside for a logo or brand mark

rubric: White space is unoccupied area and can be any color.
Equating it with literal white is the common misconception.

items.prompt: Which of the following are recognized design principles? Select all that apply.

options.label: Contrast
Alignment
Repetition
Bleed
Rasterizing

rubric: Contrast, alignment and repetition are core design principles.
Bleed and rasterizing are production or file terms, not principles.

items.prompt: A designer is preparing a poster for a print shop. The printer asks her to extend the background image slightly past the trim edge so no white slivers show after cutting. What is this extra area called?

options.label: Kerning
Gutter
Bleed
Margin

rubric: Bleed is artwork extending past the trim line.
A margin is the inside safe area and a gutter is the space between columns.

items.prompt: Why do designers usually make a heading noticeably larger than the body text?

options.label: To fill more of the page area
To show importance and guide reading order
To make the page look more decorative and eye-catching
To reduce the number of colors needed

rubric: Size differences create hierarchy and direct the eye.
Filling space or decoration is not the purpose.

items.prompt: A slide uses light gray text on a white background. What is the most likely result?

options.label: The text will look elegant and stand out
The text will look larger than it is
The text will look softer, so it reads more easily and calmly
The text will be hard to read from low contrast

rubric: Low contrast between text and background reduces legibility.
Soft gray is often wrongly thought to look refined at no cost.

items.prompt: A poster pairs blue and orange for high energy. How are these two colors related on the color wheel?

options.label: They are tints and shades of one hue
They are evenly spaced, called triadic
They sit opposite, called complementary
They sit side by side, called analogous

rubric: Blue and orange are opposite, making them complementary.
Analogous colors sit side by side.

items.prompt: Why do designers usually limit a design to two or three typefaces?

options.label: Fewer fonts keep the design consistent and cohesive
Most software slows down or crashes when a file uses more fonts
Print shops charge extra for every additional typeface used
Readers trust a design more when each line uses its own font

rubric: Limiting fonts keeps a unified look.
The other options are invented technical or cost reasons.

items.prompt: On a flyer, a price and its product name are placed close together, away from other items. What does this proximity tell the viewer?

options.label: That they should be read last, after the other items
That they belong together as a group
That they must be set in the same typeface
That they are less important than distant items

rubric: Closeness signals relationship.
Position near each other says nothing about importance or font.

items.prompt: Which choices generally make a long paragraph of body text easier to read? Select all that apply.

options.label: Setting the paragraph in all capitals
A moderate line length
Centering every line
Dark text on a light background
Comfortable line spacing

rubric: Strong contrast, comfortable spacing and moderate line length aid reading.
All caps and centering slow reading by removing word shapes and a steady left edge.

items.prompt: A student's event flyer has the title, date, details and sponsors all centered, all in the same size and weight, and packed edge to edge. Viewers say they cannot tell what matters. Which change best addresses this?

options.label: Add a second decorative font to the title only
Change all of the text to a brighter color
Make the title large and bold, details smaller
Shrink all the text equally to add more margin

rubric: Varying size and weight creates hierarchy so the key message is seen first.
Adding fonts, shrinking, or recoloring everything does not distinguish importance.

items.prompt: What does visual hierarchy do in a design?

options.label: It guides the eye through content in order of importance
It arranges elements in strict symmetry so the left and right halves match exactly
It limits a design to one typeface so that all text looks consistent in every section
It gives every element the same prominence so that no content is favored over other content

rubric: Hierarchy uses size, weight and color to signal what to read first, second and third.
Distractors confuse hierarchy with equal emphasis, symmetry or a single typeface.

items.prompt: A flyer places each event date directly beneath its title, with larger gaps between one event and the next. Which principle is mainly at work, and why?

options.label: Contrast, because dates differ strongly from the titles above them
Proximity, because nearby items are read as related to each other
Repetition, because the same style recurs for each event
Symmetry, because the events mirror one another down the page

rubric: Proximity groups related items through closeness, and gaps separate groups.
Distractors name other real principles that do not explain the spacing.

items.prompt: Why is light gray text on a white background hard to read?

options.label: Gray is a warm color that advances and blurs the letter edges on screen
Too little contrast between text and background reduces legibility
Gray and white are complementary colors, so they vibrate when placed together
Light text only stays readable at any size when set in a serif typeface

rubric: Legibility depends on the difference in lightness between text and background.
Distractors misuse color-theory terms or blame the typeface style.

items.prompt: A palette uses blue, blue-green and green, which sit next to each other on the color wheel. How is this scheme classified?

options.label: Monochromatic
Analogous
Complementary
Triadic

rubric: Neighboring hues form an analogous scheme.
Monochromatic uses one hue only, and complementary or triadic schemes use hues far apart.

items.prompt: What is the main job of whitespace (negative space) in a layout?

options.label: It reserves blank areas for content that will be added once the design is finished
It marks zones where a background color must always be applied so text keeps enough contrast
It cuts printing cost because blank areas use far less ink than filled ones, which is why designers add it
It separates and frames content so the layout feels less cluttered and is easier to scan

rubric: Whitespace gives content room to breathe and helps the eye group and scan it.
Distractors treat whitespace as unused leftover space or a cost measure.

items.prompt: Which of these are effects of consistently aligning elements to a shared edge? Select all that apply.

options.label: Related items appear visually connected across the page
The design becomes perfectly symmetrical
Size and weight differences no longer matter for emphasis
The layout looks more organized and deliberate

rubric: A shared edge creates order and an invisible line linking items.
Alignment does not create symmetry or replace hierarchy.

items.prompt: A student's poster uses a script font for the title, a different script for dates, a bold slab font for body text, and two more fonts for captions. It looks messy to viewers. Which explanation best accounts for this?

options.label: The type is set too large, which shrinks the whitespace around lines and crowds the layout
Too many unrelated typefaces compete, so no consistent system signals each text role
Bold body text is heavier than the captions, which breaks the contrast between text levels
Script fonts are decorative and hard to read, so they should be avoided on most posters

rubric: Limiting typefaces and using them consistently by role gives a cohesive look.
Distractors offer absolute rules or blame size and weight rather than the lack of a system.

items.prompt: You are setting body text on a dark navy slide background. Which text color should you choose for readability?

options.label: Medium blue
Saturated red
Dark gray
Off-white

rubric: Light text on a dark background gives high contrast.
Medium blue, dark gray and saturated red are close in value to navy or vibrate against it.

items.prompt: You are setting a paragraph of 12pt body text for a printed handout. Which line spacing (leading) is the best starting point?

options.label: 14 to 18pt
6pt
30pt
12pt, with no extra space

rubric: Leading of about 120-150% of the type size keeps lines distinct yet connected.
Tighter spacing makes lines collide and much wider spacing breaks the paragraph apart.

items.prompt: A slide is mostly shades of blue. You need a call-to-action button that stands out strongly. Which button color is the best choice?

options.label: Orange
Light blue
Navy
Teal

rubric: Orange is blue's complement, so it contrasts strongly with the palette.
The other options are close to the existing hues and would blend in.

items.prompt: You are placing a photo of a runner on a square social graphic, using the rule of thirds. Where should the runner go?

options.label: Dead center of the frame, with equal empty space on every side
Against the right edge, facing out of the frame toward the edge
On the left vertical third line, facing toward the open space on the right
In the bottom corner, partly cropped, with the rest of the frame left empty

rubric: Placing the subject on a third line and facing into open space gives balanced, dynamic composition.
Centered, edge-facing or cropped placements weaken balance or lead the eye out.

items.prompt: You are laying out a poster for a jazz night. Which size order, largest to smallest, best supports a clear hierarchy?

options.label: Venue address, date and time, event name, sponsor fine print
Sponsor logos, event name, venue address, date and time
Date and time, sponsor fine print, event name, venue address
Event name, date and time, venue address, sponsor fine print

rubric: The event name is the main message, followed by the key details and then the fine print.
Distractors give prominence to secondary details over the main message.

items.prompt: A slide has nine bullet points, four typefaces, and text placed directly over a busy photo. Which changes would improve it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cut the text to three or four key points
Add a decorative border around every bullet point
Put a solid panel behind the text that sits over the photo
Shrink the text so all nine bullets fit comfortably
Limit the slide to one or two typefaces

rubric: Fewer points, fewer typefaces and a solid backing panel reduce clutter and improve legibility.
Shrinking text and adding borders increase clutter.

items.prompt: A social graphic has a centered title, a left-aligned subtitle, and a right-aligned logo, each sitting at a different margin. It looks haphazard. Which fix best applies the alignment principle?

options.label: Enlarge the logo until it matches the title so that they carry equal weight
Add a thin border around each element to hold it in place on the page
Center the title and set the subtitle in a second typeface for variety
Left-align the title, subtitle and logo to one shared margin

rubric: Aligning all elements to one edge creates order and a clear reading path.
Distractors add variety, size changes or borders without fixing the misaligned edges.

items.prompt: A poster uses 16pt body text. You apply a modular type scale with a ratio of 1.5, so each step up is the previous size times 1.5. Which pair gives the subtitle and title sizes?

options.label: Subtitle 24pt, title 32pt
Subtitle 26pt, title 40pt
Subtitle 20pt, title 24pt
Subtitle 24pt, title 36pt

rubric: Each step multiplies by 1.5: 16 to 24 to 36.
Distractors use additive or arbitrary increments instead of a constant ratio.

items.prompt: You must place white headline text over a busy mid-tone photograph on a social graphic. Which step most reliably makes the text legible while keeping the photo visible?

options.label: Increase the photo's saturation so the text stands out more
Make the headline bolder and add a thin white outline to it
Switch the headline to a light gray to soften the contrast
Add a semi-transparent dark overlay on the photo behind the text

rubric: A dark overlay raises value contrast between text and background.
Outlines, softer grays or saturation do not fix low value contrast on a busy mid-tone.

items.prompt: A slide palette has a light gray neutral used as the background, a dark navy brand color and a bright orange accent. Applying the 60-30-10 proportion with the neutral background as the dominant color, which allocation is correct?

options.label: Equal thirds of gray, navy and orange
60% navy, 30% orange, 10% light gray
60% orange, 30% navy, 10% light gray
60% light gray, 30% navy, 10% orange

rubric: The dominant neutral takes most area, a secondary color supports, and the accent is used sparingly.
Distractors give the bright accent a large share, which dilutes its emphasis.

items.prompt: A layout uses a 12-column grid. Each content card is set to span 4 columns. How many cards fit side by side in one row?
rubric: 12 divided by 4 gives 3 cards per row.
Other values come from dividing by the wrong span or miscounting.

items.prompt: You are setting a paragraph of 10pt body text for a printed handout. Which line spacing (leading) fits the usual guideline of roughly 120-145% of the font size?

options.label: 10pt
8pt
14pt
22pt

rubric: 14pt is 140% of 10pt, within the comfortable range.
Solid or tight leading crowds lines, and very loose leading breaks the paragraph into separate lines.

items.prompt: A flyer has the event date at the top, the venue at the bottom, and the contact details sitting close to unrelated sponsor logos. Which changes apply the proximity principle correctly? Select all that apply.

options.label: Center all elements so they feel related by alignment
Leave more space between unrelated groups than within a group
Add equal spacing between every line so nothing is favored
Group the date, time and venue together as one block

rubric: Proximity means related items sit together and unrelated groups are separated by more space.
Equal spacing or centering everything erases the grouping cues.

items.prompt: You are finishing an A5 flyer with a full-color blue background that runs to the page edge. The printer will trim the sheets after printing, and a headline sits 2mm from the trim line. What should you do before exporting the print file?

options.label: Add a thin white border around the page so trimming errors are not visible
Keep the layout and ask the printer to trim slightly inside the headline
Extend the background past the trim by a few millimeters and move the headline inside a safe margin
Shrink the background so it stops exactly at the trim line and leave the headline where it is

rubric: Bleed prevents white slivers after trimming, and a safe margin protects text from being cut.
Stopping at the trim line or adding borders ignores normal trim variation.

items.prompt: A poster feels cluttered. The title, three subheads and the date are all bold, uppercase and nearly the same size. What is the most likely root cause?

options.label: Every element has the same emphasis, so there is no clear hierarchy
The poster uses too few colors, so the flat palette gives the eye no focal point
The margins are too large, which pushes the text into a tight central cluster
The typeface is too narrow, so the letters and lines look crowded together

rubric: When every element has the same emphasis, the eye has no entry point.
Typeface width, color count and margins do not explain uniform emphasis.

items.prompt: A slide shows saturated red text on a saturated green background. It appears to shimmer and is tiring to read, even though the hues are very different. What best explains this?

options.label: The two colors have similar lightness, so hue difference alone gives weak legibility
The background is so saturated that it overpowers the text and reduces its legibility
The colors sit too far apart on the color wheel, so their contrast clashes and tires the eye
Red text has a long wavelength, which the eye focuses poorly on and so reads with difficulty

rubric: Legibility relies mainly on value (lightness) contrast, which is low here.
Hue distance, red itself or saturation alone do not account for the vibration.

items.prompt: A slide has a five-line paragraph of body text that is center-aligned. Viewers say it is tiring to read. Which analysis best explains why?

options.label: Center-aligned text must be set in a smaller size than the headline, which strains the eye
The ragged left edge gives the eye no consistent starting point on each line
Centered lines make the text block wider than the title, which breaks the slide's hierarchy
The text looks too symmetrical, which makes the slide feel static and uninteresting

rubric: Reading multi-line text relies on returning to a consistent left edge.
Width, font-size and symmetry arguments miss the readability mechanism.

items.prompt: A brochure pairs two similar serif typefaces, one for headings and one for body text. Reviewers say it looks like a mistake rather than a deliberate choice. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Two typefaces are too many for a brochure, so the layout should be limited to a single face
The faces are too alike to contrast, so the difference reads as an error
Serif faces clash when paired, because their matching strokes compete for attention at every size
The heading face is lighter than the body face, so the hierarchy is lost and headings fade

rubric: Pairings need clear contrast in structure, weight or style, or a single family.
Banning serif pairs or limiting to one face is a rigid rule, not the cause.

items.prompt: A banner has a large dark photo filling the right half and a small block of light, thin text on the left half. It feels lopsided. What is the best analysis?

options.label: The dark image has far more visual weight than the light text, with no counterweight
The two halves use different colors, so adding more colors to the text would make them match
The text sits on the left, where readers give less attention, so the layout reads as weaker
The photo is too wide to fit within the grid columns, so it breaks the layout structure

rubric: Dark, large, detailed elements carry more visual weight than small light text.
Position bias, grid fit and color count do not explain the imbalance.

items.prompt: On a web banner, the call-to-action button gets ignored in testing. Which factors could plausibly explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Its color has little contrast with the banner background
A larger, bolder headline nearby competes for the same attention
It uses a sans-serif typeface, which is always overlooked
Whitespace around it makes it too easy to find

rubric: Low contrast and competing emphasis both weaken a focal element.
Whitespace usually helps isolation, and sans-serif type is not inherently ignored.

items.prompt: A presentation slide shows a line chart with five series, each in a different bright color of equal thickness, plus a 40pt title. The takeaway is that only series C is rising, yet audience members cannot tell what matters. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: Five series is too many for one chart, so each should get its own small chart
Line charts cannot show a trend clearly once more than three series share one plot
All series have equal visual weight, so nothing signals which carries the message
The 40pt title is too large and pulls attention away from the chart's lines to itself

rubric: Emphasis should be directed, for example by muting other series and highlighting C.
Adding colors worsens the competition, and the title size or series limit is not the cause.

items.prompt: A poster has a 60pt bold headline, a 24pt subhead and 12pt grey body text, yet viewers' eyes land first on a small saturated orange logo in a corner. What best explains this?

options.label: The headline's bold weight lowers its contrast, so a lighter small element automatically wins the hierarchy
The logo is the only saturated hue on a neutral page, so color contrast outweighs the headline's size advantage
Corner placements always attract attention first because readers scan the page edges before reading the center
Small elements draw the eye since the brain treats reduced size as a signal of the most important content

rubric: A lone saturated hue on a neutral field creates strong contrast that can beat size in pulling attention.
Distractors rely on false rules about corners, bold weight, or small size.

items.prompt: White 18pt text sits over a photo darkened with a uniform 30% black overlay. Some words are legible, others vanish. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The photo has bright regions beneath part of the text, so the uniform overlay leaves contrast too low only there
White text always loses legibility on photos because the eye reads dark text on light areas more quickly
The 18pt size is too small for any overlay to help, so legibility depends only on increasing font weight
A uniform overlay flattens the photo's color, which lowers the text contrast across the whole line equally

rubric: Uneven luminance in the photo means a uniform overlay gives uneven contrast, failing only where the image is bright.
Distractors blame a blanket rule, size alone, or uniform loss, which cannot explain partial legibility.

items.prompt: A narrow 2-inch column of justified 11pt body text shows uneven word spacing and white gaps running down the paragraph. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: The typeface is a serif, and serif letterforms create uneven word spacing whenever text is justified
The line spacing is too loose, which pulls word gaps on adjacent lines apart and makes them look like channels
Few characters fit per line, so justification must stretch word spaces unevenly to fill each line
The text size is too small, so the spaces look proportionally larger than they would at bigger sizes

rubric: Short measures give justification little room to adjust, causing uneven spacing and rivers.
Distractors blame leading, serifs, or size, which are not the root cause.

items.prompt: A slide uses saturated red text on a saturated green panel of near-equal lightness. It appears to shimmer and some viewers cannot read it. What is the core problem?

options.label: Both colors are highly saturated, so lowering saturation on each, while keeping their lightness equal, would fix legibility
Red is warm and green is cool, so the temperature clash pulls the eye apart and makes small lettering hard to read
The two hues are complementary, so they partly cancel each other's saturation and the text blends into the panel
The hues differ but their lightness is nearly equal, so there is little value contrast for edges to hold

rubric: Legibility depends mainly on value (lightness) contrast; equal lightness causes vibration and fails for color-blind viewers.
Distractors misattribute the problem to hue theory or saturation alone.

items.prompt: A two-column slide has equal column widths. The left holds a dense dark paragraph, the right a pale, light-toned icon. The slide feels lopsided. Why?

options.label: The icon sits on the right, and the eye reads right-side content as less important regardless of its tone
Equal widths create static symmetry, and symmetry always reads as lopsided unless columns follow the golden ratio
Dense text creates loose leading, which makes the left column look visually wider than its measured width
Visual weight differs: the dark text mass pulls harder than the pale icon, so the composition tips left

rubric: Balance depends on visual weight (tone, density), not measured geometry alone.
Distractors invoke ratio myths, reading-side myths, or leading mistakes.

items.prompt: A flyer follows a clean 12-column grid but still feels cluttered. Which observations would explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Equal margins on all sides always read as crowded
Three type families and six sizes compete, blurring the hierarchy
Nine different gaps between groups mean proximity does not signal which items belong together
Every block has the same size and weight, so no focal point emerges
Using a grid limits whitespace and forces elements to touch one another

rubric: Inconsistent proximity, too many type variations, and no focal point all produce clutter even on a grid.
Grids do not force touching elements, and equal margins are not inherently crowded.

items.prompt: A designer makes a square social graphic: centered headline, centered photo, centered body copy, and a small centered 'Sign up' button in the same grey as the body copy. Testers read everything but few notice the button. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: Square formats shorten viewing time, so call-to-action buttons tend to work better in vertical layouts than in square ones
The photo is too large, and an image filling over half the canvas pulls attention from action elements placed near it
Centered alignment weakens buttons, since viewers tend to notice actions aligned to the left edge of a layout first
The button matches the body copy's color and weight with no distinct contrast or space, so it reads as more text

rubric: A call to action needs distinct contrast, size or space; matching surrounding text makes it blend in.
Distractors cite unfounded rules about alignment, image size, and format.

items.prompt: An annual report with long tables and dense text is printed at 9pt. Criteria: stay legible at small sizes and look professional. Which type pairing is the best choice?

options.label: A decorative script for headings and a thin display sans for body, because the contrast adds personality at small sizes
A condensed ultra-light face throughout, because narrow letterforms fit more tables on each page without extra pages
A sturdy serif for body text with a clean sans for headings and table figures, because both hold up small and differ by role
Two similar geometric sans faces in slightly different weights, because near-identical styles guarantee harmony everywhere

rubric: Robust, legible faces with clearly distinct roles meet both stated criteria.
Distractors sacrifice small-size legibility or create muddy, ambiguous pairings.

items.prompt: A talk will be projected in a sunlit hall on an old, washed-out projector. Criteria: readable from the back row, and the mid-tone brand blue must appear. Which palette is best?

options.label: White background with brand blue body text, because mid-tone text on white stays crisp on faded projectors and keeps the brand color prominent
Dark navy background with white text, brand blue kept for accent shapes, because high value contrast survives washout
Pale blue tint background with white text, because soft tones reduce glare from the sunlit windows and ease eye strain
Brand blue background with light grey text, because using the brand color as the ground maximizes recognition and consistency

rubric: Washed-out projection compresses mid-tones, so extreme value contrast for text with the brand color as an accent satisfies both criteria.
Distractors place mid-tone or low-contrast colors where text must be read.

items.prompt: A highway billboard is read in about three seconds. Criterion: the message must be grasped at a glance. Which flaw is the most serious?

options.label: Only two colors in the palette, which limits the emotional range available to the board
A logo at the bottom-right instead of top-left, which weakens conventional reading order on the board
A background photo that is not aligned to an underlying grid, which disrupts the structure of the layout
Thirty words of copy in a light-weight font, which exceeds what can be read in the viewing time

rubric: Excess copy and thin type directly defeat the at-a-glance criterion.
Distractors are minor stylistic concerns that do not stop the message being read.

items.prompt: A client's slide has 140 words. Constraints: 0.75-inch margins for print trimming, 24pt minimum text for the room, and the key message intact. Which response is best?

options.label: Shrink only the margins and keep 24pt, since margins are decorative and the trim risk is small
Reduce text to 16pt and margins to 0.25 inch so all content stays on one slide as supplied
Use a condensed font at 18pt so the words fit while margins and the single slide are preserved
Split it into two slides with one claim each, keeping margins and 24pt so no constraint is broken

rubric: Splitting content is the only option that satisfies margins, size and message.
Distractors break at least one stated constraint to keep one slide.

items.prompt: A junior uses five font weights and three italic styles in one 200-word card to 'show hierarchy'. Which critique is best supported by hierarchy principles?

options.label: Too many emphasis levels dilute the contrast between them; two or three distinct levels would make the order clearer
Hierarchy needs at least five levels on a card, so the design is fine but should add a sixth for completeness
Weights and italics should be avoided entirely, since hierarchy should come only from size differences among elements
Only the italics are the issue, because weight changes never compete with each other within the same block of text

rubric: Hierarchy relies on clearly distinguishable levels; too many make them indistinct.
Distractors set absolute rules or ignore competing weights.

items.prompt: A brand refresh must stay readable on small mobile screens and work in one-color print. Which design judgements are well supported by those criteria? Select all that apply.

options.label: Choose a logotype that remains distinct at 24px wide
Use a heavier, open-spaced wordmark rather than a hairline script
Rely on a subtle gradient between two similar hues to separate the logo from the ground
Encode product categories only by color so category names can be dropped
Ensure the mark works in a single solid color without losing its form

rubric: Small-size distinctness, single-color robustness and sturdy letterforms all meet the stated criteria.
Gradients and color-only coding fail in one-color print and for accessibility.

items.prompt: A client demands doubling the logo on a landing page. The logo is already clear, the headline carries the main message, and analytics show visitors skim the headline. Criteria: preserve hierarchy and keep brand recognition. What is the best response?

options.label: Move the logo into the headline line and match its size, so both messages share equal emphasis on the page
Increase it modestly and add contrast or clear space, so recognition improves without overtaking the headline
Refuse any change, because hierarchy rules fix the logo at the smallest size that remains legible on the page
Double it as requested, because the client's brand recognition goals outweigh any hierarchy concerns on a landing page

rubric: A modest boost with contrast or space serves the client's concern while keeping the headline dominant.
Distractors ignore one criterion or flatten the hierarchy.

items.prompt: A poster headline is set in saturated red on a saturated blue background. The designer says the hue difference guarantees strong contrast. Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Red and blue sit too near each other on the wheel, so a true complementary pair would guarantee strong contrast
Hue difference is not luminance contrast; with similar lightness the edges shimmer and the letters are hard to read
Contrast is fine, but the red should be set in a thinner weight so the blue behind it shows through more
Saturated colors always read well together, so the real problem is only that the headline is set too large

rubric: Legibility depends mainly on lightness difference, and equal-lightness saturated hues vibrate.
Distractors treat hue contrast or complementarity as a substitute for luminance contrast.

items.prompt: A flyer has a 28-character-wide text column and no hyphenation available. Criteria: even word spacing and a clean, calm text edge. Which setting is the best judgement?

options.label: Centered, because symmetric lines hide the uneven gaps that a narrow measure would otherwise create
Justified, with tight tracking, because a straight right edge always looks more professional in any column
Justified, with letterspacing expanded on loose lines so every line reaches both edges of the column
Left-aligned and ragged-right, with line breaks adjusted by hand to avoid very short or very long lines

rubric: Narrow justified columns without hyphenation produce rivers and uneven spacing; ragged-right keeps spacing constant.
Distractors assume justification or centering is neutral or tidier regardless of measure.

items.prompt: A slide has a title, three statistics, a subtitle and a logo, all in bold type of 40pt or larger and in different colors. Criterion: a single clear reading order with the fewest changes. Which fix is best?

options.label: Give each element a colored border and equal padding so every item is clearly separated from the others on the slide
Make the key statistic dominant in size and weight, and set everything else in one shared, quieter style
Increase every element's size further so that nothing on the slide can be missed by the audience
Add a different accent color to each statistic so viewers can tell the three figures apart quickly

rubric: Hierarchy needs one dominant entry point and a consistent secondary tier.
Distractors add more emphasis, which flattens hierarchy further.

items.prompt: A brand allows only two typefaces on a report cover. Criteria: each face has a clearly distinct role, and the pair feels coherent. Which pairing is the best judgement?

options.label: Two display scripts with different personalities, so both the title and subtitle stand out strongly
A humanist serif for text and a neutral sans for headings, with matching x-heights and clear role contrast
One traditional serif for the title and a similar transitional serif for the subtitle, for a subtle contrast
Two different geometric sans-serifs of similar weight, since matching styles guarantee a coherent look

rubric: Clear structural contrast with compatible proportions gives distinct roles and coherence.
Near-identical faces look like a mistake; two display faces compete.

items.prompt: A designer centers a circle and a square of identical width in a row of icons, and the circle looks smaller. Criterion: icons should appear equal in visual size. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Leave them identical, because measured dimensions are the only objective basis for alignment and sizing
Scale the circle slightly larger, because equal measured width does not give equal perceived size
Add a thicker outline to the circle only, so that its measured width matches the square's exactly
Shrink the square slightly, since the circle is the shape that sets the correct size for the row

rubric: Round shapes need overshoot because they have less area at the same bounding width.
Distractors rely on literal measurement over optical perception.

items.prompt: A slide with 12pt light gray (#BBBBBB) body paragraphs on white will be projected in a bright room for a large audience. Criterion: legibility from the back row. Which critiques are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Gray on white gives too little luminance contrast for a bright room
Centering every paragraph would improve scanning speed for long text
Twelve-point text is too small for the back row, so size up and cut words
Adding a soft drop shadow to the gray text would restore adequate contrast
Splitting the content into slides with one idea each addresses the density

rubric: Low contrast, small size and density all hurt remote legibility.
Shadows and centering do not fix contrast or density.

items.prompt: A client insists on its brand light orange (#FF9F40) for the 9pt captions on a white annual report. Criteria: captions must be comfortably legible in print and the brand color must still be recognisable. Which recommendation is best?

options.label: Switch all captions to pure black and remove orange completely, because legibility outranks any brand color
Keep orange captions and darken the white page slightly, since a tinted page raises caption contrast
Use the orange for captions but set them in bold italics, since extra weight offsets the low contrast
Use the orange for rules, icons and large headings, and set captions in a dark neutral for legibility

rubric: Orange stays visible as an accent while small text gets high contrast.
Distractors either keep failing contrast or discard the brand unnecessarily.

items.prompt: Design a type system for a poster read from 3 meters. Constraints: one type family, exactly three clear levels, and levels distinguishable at distance. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: One family with a bold headline at about 6x body size, a medium subhead at about 2.5x, and regular body text
One family, five sizes in small steps from 40pt to 52pt, so every level feels related to the others
One family in a single weight, with all three levels at the same size and separated only by color
Two families for contrast: a display face for the headline and a sans for the subhead and body text

rubric: Large scale steps and weight make three levels distinct from a distance within one family.
Distractors break the family limit, the level count, or the distinction requirement.

items.prompt: Create a chart palette for four data series. Constraints: it must stay distinguishable when printed in grayscale and for readers with red-green color blindness. Which design meets both?

options.label: Four closely spaced shades of one gray, since grayscale printing then changes nothing about the series
Four fully saturated hues spaced evenly around the color wheel, since hue spacing gives separation
Dark blue, light yellow, mid orange and pale blue, varying in lightness, plus direct labels
Red, green, orange and brown at equal brightness, each series identified in a chart legend

rubric: Varying lightness survives grayscale and color-vision differences; blue/yellow avoids red-green confusion.
Equal-lightness hues collapse in grayscale; red-green sets fail for color-blind readers.

items.prompt: A social graphic must work as both a 1:1 post and a 4:5 post from one master file. Constraints: no text may be cropped, and the background should fill each format. Which build meets both?

options.label: Keep all text inside a central 1:1 safe area and extend the background art to the full 4:5 height
Center the text block in the 4:5 frame and let the 1:1 export crop the top and bottom of the canvas
Spread the text to the full-width edges of the frame, then scale the whole file down for the 1:1 export
Fit the text inside the 4:5 frame with its own margins and export the 1:1 by cropping the sides evenly

rubric: A safe area common to both crops with bleed art meets both constraints.
Distractors risk cropping text or ignore the single-master constraint.

items.prompt: A concert poster has well-aligned margins, consistent type and three photos of equal size and weight. Viewers say they do not know where to look first. What is the design missing?

options.label: A fourth photo of the same size, so that the layout's symmetry becomes more balanced and even
A thin border around each photo, so that every image is clearly separated from its neighbors on the page
A second typeface on the headline, so that the text competes less with the photographs for attention
A dominant focal element, such as one enlarged photo, that sets an entry point and reading order

rubric: Equal weight gives no entry point; a dominant element creates hierarchy.
Distractors add elements without establishing visual priority.

items.prompt: A headline must sit over a busy full-bleed photo. Constraints: keep the photo full-bleed, add no text box or panel, and keep the headline legible. Which fix meets all three?

options.label: Reduce the headline's opacity to 50%, so that the photo detail shows through the lettering
Add a heavy black outline to the letters, so that the edges stand out against any part of the photo
Place the headline in the photo's quietest area and add a subtle gradient scrim beneath it
Blur the entire photograph strongly, so that the background no longer competes with the text

rubric: Using a calm region plus a gradual scrim keeps the photo and text legible without a box.
Blurring ruins the photo; outlines look crude; transparency lowers contrast.

items.prompt: You must design a slide template that non-designers will fill in without breaking the brand look. Which elements should the template include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A fixed grid with defined margins and locked placeholder positions
Preset layouts for common content types, such as a title, comparison and chart
A free color picker on every object so each team can personalise slides
Unlimited font choices so authors can match the tone of each topic
A small set of preset text styles with set sizes and hierarchy

rubric: Constraints (grid, styles, layouts) guide non-designers to consistent results.
Free color and font choices invite inconsistency.

items.prompt: A logo must be used from a 16px browser favicon up to a billboard. The full lockup has a thin-line emblem, a long wordmark and a tagline. Constraints: stay recognisable at every size and keep the brand identity consistent. Which design plan meets both?

options.label: Create a system with the full lockup for large uses and a simplified emblem-only mark for tiny sizes
Redraw the wordmark in bold for every size, and drop the emblem so that the logo is only text
Use a different, unrelated icon for the favicon, since small sizes need their own distinct identity
Scale the full lockup down uniformly and rely on screens to sharpen the thin lines at 16px

rubric: A responsive logo system keeps shared core shapes while simplifying detail for small sizes.
Distractors either fail legibility at 16px or break consistency.
